prime.problem: You run an agent 3 times on each of 30 tasks, get 90 pass/fail scores, and put the textbook error bar on the pass rate. The bar comes out too short, because 3 trials of one task mostly agree. And when you compare two agents with two separate bars, a real gain disappears into the overlap. Either way you end up trusting noise or missing real progress.
prime.fits: Second statistics card of the evidence course. Measuring an agent gave you a by-task interval for one agent; pass@k vs pass^k showed what repeats measure. This card says why grouping by task is the honest bar, and how to compare two agents on the same tasks.
expect: clustered standard error (one cluster per task)
paired differences and the covariance they cancel
coverage: does a 95% bar contain the truth 95% of the time?
prime.goal: Compute a clustered bar for one agent and a paired bar for the gain between two agents from a tasks × trials grid, and explain why the naive bar is too short and the unpaired one too long.

attend: Which term in the clustered formula grows when two trials of the same task both pass or both fail?
Why does the clustered SE for 30 tasks × 3 trials come out almost equal to the SE of the 30 per-task means?
In the paired formula, which quantity cancels, and why is it positive whenever two agents find the same tasks hard?
Why did the unpaired bar cover the true gain 99.7% of the time, and why is that a problem rather than a bonus?
If both bars are honest, why does the paired one still find a real 9-point gain only about a third of the time?

must: Trials of one task share its difficulty → their scores agree → 90 trials carry much less information than 90 independent scores → the plain SE (s ÷ √90) is too short (0.052 vs a real spread of 0.069) and its 95% bar covers the truth only 85% of the time

Clustered SE adds the within-task cross products (s<sub>ic</sub> − s̄)(s<sub>jc</sub> − s̄) → agreement inside a task makes them positive → the bar widens (1.34× here) → with equal-size clusters it is almost the SE of the per-task means, which is Miller's recipe for K repeats

Both agents ran the same tasks → their per-task scores correlate (0.63 here) → Var(B − A) = Var A + Var B − 2 Cov removes the shared difficulty → the bar on the gain shrinks (0.095 → 0.059) → a real gain is called real far more often (35.8% vs 7.6%)

More trials per task shrink only the within-task noise → the plain SE keeps falling while the real spread is held up by task-to-task difficulty → the naive bar gets more wrong as you add trials (65.5% coverage at 10 trials) → add tasks, not trials, to tighten the bar
elevated: Both honest bars still use 1.96 from the normal approximation → at 30 tasks they cover 93.5–94.1%, not 95% → Bowyer et al. say CLT-style bars are too narrow below about 100 questions and suggest Bayesian intervals
reference: the exact triple-sum form of Miller's clustered SE
the simulation's illustrative task population (logit mean 0.3, spread 1.8, B shifted by +0.6)

compress.prompt: Card closed. In 3–5 sentences, explain why the plain error bar is too short for a tasks × trials eval and what fixes it, then why comparing two agents task by task gives a shorter bar than two separate bars. Or draw the chain: shared difficulty → agreeing trials → … → paired gain.
checklist: trials of one task share its difficulty, so they are not independent scores
the plain SE treats 90 trials as 90 independent scores, so it is too short (85% coverage)
clustered SE adds back the within-task agreement; it is about the SE of the per-task means
paired: per-task differences cancel the shared difficulty, the 2 Cov term
unpaired bars on the gain are too wide, so real gains get missed
more tasks shrink the honest bar; more trials mostly shrink only the naive one

retrieve.q: Your teammate reports "57.8% ± 5.2 points (1 SE), 90 runs" for an agent run 3 times on 30 tasks. Explain what is wrong with that bar and what the honest number is.
answer: the 90 runs are 30 groups of 3 that share a task's difficulty, not 90 independent scores
the bar must be clustered by task: 0.070, so ±7.0 points per SE, 1.34× wider
the 95% bar becomes 44.0% to 71.6% instead of 47.5% to 68.0%

retrieve.q: Walk through the paired comparison on the example: what is the data point for each task, which variances go in, and how do you get 0.059?
answer: per task: B's pass rate over its 3 trials minus A's
SE = √(0.103 ÷ 30) = 0.059; the 95% bar on the +0.122 gain is +0.007 to +0.237, so it excludes zero

retrieve.q: You have budget for 270 more agent runs. Do you run the same 30 tasks 9 more times each, or add 90 new tasks at 3 trials each? Justify with what each one shrinks.
answer: extra trials only average away within-task noise; the task-to-task difficulty spread stays
at 10 trials on 30 tasks the real spread of the score only fell from 0.069 to 0.059
new tasks shrink the difficulty term too (100 tasks × 3: real spread 0.037), so add tasks first, unless the goal is a per-task reliability like pass^k

retrieve.q: When should you not use the paired bar, and what do you use instead?
answer: when the two agents were scored on different task sets, or with different graders: use the unpaired difference, √(SE<sub>A</sub>² + SE<sub>B</sub>²)
when the agents disagree on which tasks are hard (correlation near 0), pairing is still valid but gains nothing
at small n (under ~100 tasks), consider a Bayesian interval in either case

compare.q: That card built a by-task interval for 10 tasks × 3 trials using a t value of 2.262; this card builds a clustered SE with Miller's triple sum. What is fundamentally the same, what differs, and when would they disagree?
answer: same idea: the task, not the trial, is the independent unit; both average each task's trials first
with equal-size clusters, the clustered SE ≈ the SE of the per-task means (0.0704 vs 0.0714 here)
the earlier card used t for 9 degrees of freedom because 10 tasks is tiny; the clustered formula uses 1.96, which is too narrow at small n
they differ when clusters are bigger than one task (tasks sharing a repo) or unequal in size: then only the clustered formula handles it directly

compare.q: GRPO subtracts the group mean from each rollout's reward; a paired comparison subtracts agent A's score from agent B's on each task. What does each subtraction cancel, and why does it reduce variance in both cases?
answer: both remove a shared, task-level term: how hard this prompt or task is
GRPO: rollouts on the same prompt share its difficulty, so reward minus the group mean leaves how much better this rollout did
paired eval: two agents on the same task share its difficulty, so B − A leaves the agent effect; the 2 Cov term is what cancels
both fail when there is little shared signal: a group where every rollout gets the same reward gives zero advantage, and agents that disagree on difficulty get nothing from pairing

compare.q: pass^k and the pass rate are both computed from the same tasks × trials grid. Why does an error bar on either one have to treat the task as the unit, and how does the meaning of the k trials differ between the two?
answer: in both, a task's trials share its difficulty, so the independent unit is the task
the pass rate averages trials to estimate a task's chance; pass^k asks whether every trial of a task succeeds
so more trials sharpen each task's estimate but cannot replace more tasks in either bar

predict.q: Keep 30 tasks, but raise the trials per task from 3 to 10 (270 runs per agent). Before running it: does the plain SE shrink, does the real spread of the score shrink as much, and what happens to the naive bar's coverage?
predict.answer: The plain SE nearly halves (0.052 → 0.029) because it sees 270 "independent" scores. The real spread only falls from 0.069 to 0.059, because the task-to-task difficulty doesn't average out over trials. So the naive bar gets worse: it covers the truth 65.5% of the time instead of 85.2%. The clustered bar stays honest (93.4%), and the paired test now finds the gain 81.0% of the time: in this simulation the per-task gain is fairly steady, so most of the gain's variance was trial noise. Real agents may not be that steady.

apply.task: Break the clustering on purpose. In stack-4-evidence/code/error-bars.py, change the spread in draw_tasks from rng.normal(0.3, 1.8, n) to rng.normal(0.3, 0.0, n), so every task has the same difficulty, and rerun. Predict first: what will the cluster/naive ratio and the naive coverage become, and will pairing still beat unpaired?
apply.done: Your run prints a median ratio of about ×0.98, naive coverage of 94.6%, and paired and unpaired both calling the gain real about half the time (49.1% vs 49.6%). You can say in one sentence why each changed: with no shared difficulty, trials of a task are independent and the two agents share nothing for pairing to cancel.
apply.hint: Only the second number in rng.normal changes. The true gain moves to +0.137 because every task now sits at the same starting chance.

reflect: Which prediction did you get wrong: that more trials make the naive bar worse, or that the unpaired bar on the gain is too wide?
What couldn't you explain cleanly: the triple sum in the clustered formula, or why it lands near the SE of per-task means?
Which relationship is still fuzzy: shared task difficulty → positive covariance, or positive covariance → a shorter paired bar?
In your own agent evals, what besides repeats of a task should count as one cluster (same repo, same fixture, same grader)?
How many tasks do you think you'd need to call a 5-point gain real, and what would you bring to the power-analysis card to check?
